chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
title: Ballrooms in Bridgeport, Boston and Providence
summary: Crawford says the band played New England ballrooms so often it felt like home and was usually the only band on the stand.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You know, Duke Ellington was saying in a book that there were some bands up around Bridgeport and stuff in the --
Yeah, I played there many times.
-- '30s that were pretty good bands. Do you remember any of those bands?

No, maybe society or bands like that, society. Providence, Boston, Bridgeport, we were up there so often, I thought that was our home, at this ballroom. I can't call the name. Oh, it was a nice ballroom. In Bridgeport.
Well, he perhaps was right, but I don't know about bands. I don't think I heard many bands. If they were, they were white bands, and we were Negro bands. And that was a different style, you know.
What would you say is the difference in the styles between the white bands and the Black bands?
Well, I don't remember hearing white

bands up there because, when we went up there to places like Bridgeport, Boston, Providence, places like that, we were the only band on the bandstand. They didn't have many bands, you know, like couple bands on the bandstand. No, we were the only ones.
